terms.gloss: fixed, appointed, regular (of times and days)
evidence: Liv. 44.37: lūnae dēfectiō statīs temporibus fit (Lewis & Short, s.v. sistō)
terms.comment: Used in set phrases: status diēs, statum tempus, stata sacrificia; Pliny calls fevers that come back at regular intervals statae febrēs (Lewis & Short).
Of someone who keeps at a thing or is always present; assiduē is “continually, regularly”. Its first sense is “settled on the land” (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: according to the usual order, regular
evidence: cōnsulēs ōrdināriī, the regular consuls (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short): an official word, the regular as against the extraordinary.

phrases.latin: Sī tū haec assiduē faciēs, tū quidem eris āthlēta summus.
phrases.english: If you do this regularly, you’ll surely become a top athlete.
The medicine is to be taken at regular times.

sources: Lewis & Short: sisto · Lewis & Short: assiduus · Lewis & Short: ordinarius
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 60, 370.
